proof.text: Use the component-ring convention in [lem-trf-affine-etale-cover-component-criterion]: $T_Z=T/I_Z$ and $\operatorname{Spec}T_Z$ has underlying space $Z$. Thus the hypothesis says precisely that the factor algebras are quasi-acyclic, where this term means that all component rings are henselian local.

source.place: Component convention and quasi-acyclic definition, printed p. 12

proof.text: Fix a component ring $C$ of $B=B_1\otimes_R B_2$. By [lem-trf-tensor-component-from-factor-components], choose component quotients $q_j:B_j\twoheadrightarrow D_j$ and $E=D_1\otimes_R D_2\twoheadrightarrow C$, with the composite from $B$ equal to its component quotient. Each $D_j$ is henselian local by the factor hypothesis and ind-etale over $R$ by [lem-trf-component-ind-etale-local-henselian]. Write $\mathfrak p_j$ for the contraction of its maximal ideal to $R$. By [lem-trf-ind-etale-local-henselian-integral], $D_j$ is a local integral $R^h_{\mathfrak p_j}$-algebra. These are exactly the hypotheses of [lem-trf-artin-join-theorem-6-3]. Its quasi-acyclicity conclusion for $E$ makes its component ring $C$ henselian local. This proves the first conclusion for every component of $B$.

source.place: Theorem 6.3 and the local ind-etale reduction preceding Theorem 6.4, printed p. 13

proof.text: Given a maximal ideal $\mathfrak m\subset B$, let $Z$ be the connected component containing its point. By the component convention, $I_Z\subseteq\mathfrak m$, so for $C=B/I_Z$ the ideal $\mathfrak m_C=\mathfrak m/I_Z$ is maximal and $C/\mathfrak m_C=B/\mathfrak m$. Step 2 makes $C$ local, hence this is its unique maximal ideal. Apply the residue alternatives of [lem-trf-artin-join-theorem-6-3] to the factor component rings $D_1,D_2$ chosen for this $C$. If both $D_j\to C$ are nonlocal, it gives that $B/\mathfrak m=C/\mathfrak m_C$ is separably closed.

source.place: Theorem 6.3 case (1) and passage to maximal ideals in Theorem 6.4, printed p. 13

proof.text: Otherwise, one map $D_i\to C$ is local. By [lem-trf-artin-join-theorem-6-3] it is integral and the induced field extension $D_i/\mathfrak m_{D_i}\to C/\mathfrak m_C$ is algebraic.

Set $\mathfrak n=q_i^{-1}(\mathfrak m_{D_i})\subset B_i$. Surjectivity of $q_i$ gives $B_i/\mathfrak n\cong D_i/\mathfrak m_{D_i}$, a field, so $\mathfrak n$ is maximal. Locality of $D_i\to C$ and the commuting quotient maps from Step 2 give, for $b\in B_i$, $b\in\mathfrak n$ iff $q_i(b)\in\mathfrak m_{D_i}$ iff its image in $C$ is in $\mathfrak m_C$ iff its tensor image is in $\mathfrak m$. Thus $\mathfrak n=\mathfrak m\cap B_i$. The quotient isomorphisms identify the field map in Step 4 with the canonical map $B_i/\mathfrak n\to B/\mathfrak m$.

source.place: Theorem 6.4, elementary contraction and quotient identifications, printed p. 13

proof.text: Finally, $B_i\to B$ is ind-etale by base change of the other factor map $R\to B_j$, $j\ne i$. The component quotient $B\to C$ is ind-etale by [lem-trf-component-ind-etale-local-henselian], so its composite $B_i\to C$ is ind-etale by [lem-weil-pbc-ind-etale-stability]. Its maximal ideal contracts to $\mathfrak n$ by Step 5. Apply [lem-trf-ind-etale-residue-separable] to these two maximal ideals: $B_i/\mathfrak n\to C/\mathfrak m_C=B/\mathfrak m$ is separable algebraic. This supplies the additional separability absent from Theorem 6.3. Steps 3 and 6 cover all residue alternatives. If $B=0$, there are no components or maximal ideals, so both conclusions are vacuous.

title: Artin tensor theorem for henselian components, with residue-field dichotomy
statement: For a commutative ring $C$ and a connected component $Z$ of $\operatorname{Spec}C$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum], its component ring is $C_Z=C/I_Z$, where $I_Z$ is generated by the idempotents $e\in C$ with $Z\subseteq V(e)$; the canonical closed subscheme $\operatorname{Spec}C_Z$ has underlying space $Z$. Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $B_1,B_2$ ind-etale $R$-algebras [def-weil-pbc-ind-etale-algebra]. Suppose every component ring of each $B_j$ is henselian local [def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology]. Set $B=B_1\otimes_R B_2$. Every component ring of $B$ is henselian local. For every maximal ideal $\mathfrak m\subset B$, either $B/\mathfrak m$ is separably closed, or there are $j\in\{1,2\}$ and a maximal ideal $\mathfrak n\subset B_j$ with $\mathfrak n=\mathfrak m\cap B_j$ such that the induced extension $B_j/\mathfrak n\to B/\mathfrak m$ is separable algebraic.

source.place: Hübner–Schmidt, The tame site of a scheme, §6, component-ring convention on printed p. 12, and Theorem 6.4, printed p. 13, specialized to two factors. No Noetherian, normality, or strict-henselian hypothesis is imposed in Theorem 6.4.
